content: A halide is a binary compound consisting of two parts: one part is a halogen atom, and the other part is an element or radical that is less electronegative than the halogen. This combination forms compounds such as fluorides, chlorides, bromides, iodides, or astatides. Many salts are classified as halides. All Group 1 metals react with halogens to form halides, which are typically white solids. A halide ion is a halogen atom that carries a negative charge. The halide anions include fluoride (F−), chloride (Cl−), bromide (Br−), iodide (I−), and astatide (At−). These ions are present in all ionic halide salts. In organic chemistry, halides represent a functional group. Any organic compound containing a halogen atom can be considered a halide. Alkyl halides are a specific type of organic compound with the general formula R-X, where R is an alkyl group covalently bonded to a halogen atom X. Pseudohalides are compounds that mimic halides in terms of their charge and reactivity. Common examples of pseudohalides include azides (N₃⁻), isocyanates (-NCO), and cyanides (CN⁻). The detection of halogens in chemical substances can be performed using the Carius halogen method. Metal halides are widely used in high-intensity discharge (HID) lamps, commonly referred to as metal halide lamps. These lamps are frequently employed in modern street lighting due to their superior energy efficiency compared to mercury-vapor lamps and their improved color rendering compared to orange high-pressure sodium lamps. Metal halide lamps are also used in greenhouses or regions with limited sunlight to supplement natural light. However, HID lamps significantly contribute to light pollution, which is why sodium-vapor lamps are often preferred for certain applications.
